rv.q: Such is my enthusiasm for Kokandy Productions' exquisite little Chicago staging of Stephen Sondheim's "Sunday in the Park with George" that I wrote down five different opening paragraphs, or organizing principles, if you will.

This time, it’s a richly emotional, cleverly designed and musically vivid “Sunday in the Park with George,” about the creation of painter Georges Seurat’s “A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte,” the large neo-impressionist masterpiece that — so very lucky for us! — hangs a few miles away in the Art Institute.
Kokandy Production’s magnificent, intimate, almost immersive production was well worth the wait.
If the first act of Sunday in the Park with George is perfect (you heard me: it's perfect), the second is… a bit clunkier.
Kokandy has gathered those ingredients for this imaginatively staged new version.
In their unique perspective, Kokandy Productions brings Sunday in the Park with George into an original light, creating a production that feels both intimate and visually striking.
The entire Kokandy Productions team should be proud of their work, and I am grateful to have had the opportunity to have seen it.
When Kokandy’s triumvirate of Sula, Barham, and Webb take on Sondheim, it’s worth your while.
Kokandy Productions gives us this in spades.

In the end, one is left with a certain feeling that the expertly crafted square peg that is Sunday in the Park with George was never going to fit into the well-intentioned round hole envisioned by Kokandy’s production team.
Kokandy’s production answers these questions with clarity, tenderness, and powerful emotional impact.
Once again Kokandy Productions has created a masterpiece of a masterpeice in a place where I did not think it could be done, THEY DID IT!
“Sunday in the Park with George,” Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s sophisticated and deeply moving masterpiece, belongs firmly in the second category.
Kevin Webb as George himself shows us a deeply emotional and dedicated artist, even if George himself can't show it.

Ultimately Lapine and Sondheim’s opus is a theatrical tour deforce with perhaps a few hiccups that is a favorite among sophisticated theater goers who are open to experiencing a challenging score — in this case performed terrifically with great vocals and instrumentation.

cn.t: Kokandy's intimate production of Sondheim's masterwork earns widespread praise for its emotional depth and clever staging, though the cramped basement space at Chopin Theatre proves challenging for some critics.
